mainTopic: How common people's wording and local custom decide what a document means: a clause that protects a lender if land loses value, and how much a wife collects for her dowry when the כתובה lists an inflated amount.
overview: This amud shows how the חכמים read people's words and documents the way ordinary people mean them. רבי יוסי teaches that where custom inflates the dowry number in a כתובה, the wife collects only the real amount. The exception is when a קנין was made with the bride's father, as מרימר rules and as רבינא's own story shows. Next comes a man who told his heirs to give his daughter 400 זוז. The final rule is that any mention of the כתובה means a written number worth half, and only a plain 'give her' means real money. Then come sharecropper cases. רבא rules that an exaggerated penalty promise of 1,000 זוז is an אסמכתא and does not bind. When wheat was planted instead of sesame, the sharecropper gets no credit for sparing the land, and he does not keep all the extra profit, because the land helped too. Finally, נהרדעי define an עיסקא as half loan and half deposit. רבא uses the name עיסקא to show the money is for business only and does not become the manager's children's movables. רבא also rules that one עיסקא written in two documents works to the investor's loss.

steps.title: The written clause helps if the land loses value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers what a certain written clause accomplishes: it protects the lender if the pledged property goes down in value.
steps.simpleTranslation: The writing helps for a loss in value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an earlier discussion. Someone asked what a certain line in a document adds, and here the answer is given: it matters if the property loses value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the clause, the lender might be stuck with only the pledged land, even if it became worth less. Because it was written, he can collect the missing amount from the borrower's other property. So the clause is not extra words. It has a real legal effect.

keyTerms.meaning: The writing (what was written in the document)
A loss or drop in value

phrases.english: The writing is effective for depreciation.
phrases.notes: If the pledged property drops in value, this line lets the lender collect the rest from the borrower's other property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a question raised just before this section about what a written clause adds.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the use of writing this clause in the document?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It protects the lender if the pledged property loses value, so he can collect the difference.

steps.title: רבי יוסי reads a כתובה by local custom
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי also explained documents by how ordinary people talk. If local custom writes the dowry as a real debt, the wife collects it all. If custom doubles it for honor, she collects half.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי would interpret the language of ordinary people, as a ברייתא teaches: in a place where they write a כתובה like a loan, she collects like a loan. Where they double it, she collects half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new example of reading documents by everyday language, this time from רבי יוסי about the dowry written in a כתובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same written number can mean different things in different places. Where people write the real dowry amount, the wife collects the full sum, just as a lender collects a loan. Where people double the number to make the father look generous, everyone knows only half is real, so she collects half.

keyTerms.meaning: Interprets the wording of ordinary people (not the language of the תורה)
A loan; here, a real debt collected in full

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the rule that local custom decides how to read the amount in a document. That rule drives the rest of the section.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei would expound common language.
phrases.notes: He means everyday phrases people put in contracts, read the way ordinary people mean them.

phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Yosei says:
In a place where they were accustomed to make a marriage contract like a loan –
she collects like a loan.
Where the custom is to double – she collects half.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן הֶדְיוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another sage who interpreted ordinary people's language in documents, after the earlier examples.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: How much of the dowry a wife collects follows local writing custom: the full amount where it is written as a real debt, half where the custom is to double it.

steps.title: נהרבלא collected one-third; מרימר collected the added amount too
steps.stepSummary: The scholars of נהרבלא let a wife collect only a third of the written dowry, but מרימר let her collect even the extra amount added for honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: The people of נהרבלא collected a third. מרימר let her collect the added value too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how the courts actually ruled. One place follows the custom rule, and מרימר rules differently, which sets up the challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In נהרבלא people wrote three times the real amount, so following רבי יוסי's logic the wife got one-third. מרימר went further and let her collect the honor amount as well. That seems to clash with the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: The added amount (the extra written for honor)

phrases.english: The people of Neharbela collected one-third,
phrases.notes: Their custom was to write three times the real amount, so the real part is one-third.

phrases.english: Mareimar would have her collect the added value as well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוסי's custom rule in practice and introduces מרימר's broader ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נהרבלא gave one-third (their custom tripled the amount). מרימר allowed collection of the full written amount, including the honor addition.

steps.title: רבינא challenges מרימר from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks מרימר: the ברייתא says that where the custom is to double, she collects only half, so how can you give her the extra?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to מרימר: But a ברייתא teaches that where they double, she collects half!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks מרימר's ruling by quoting the ברייתא of רבי יוסי from step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא clearly limits the wife to the real amount when the written number was inflated by custom. מרימר's ruling gives her the inflated part too, which looks like it goes against a tannaitic source.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Mareimar,
But isn't it taught: where they double, she collects half!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges מרימר's ruling from step 3 using the ברייתא in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: מרימר's ruling that the wife collects the honor addition too
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא limits her to half where the custom doubles the amount, so the inflated part should not be collectible.

steps.title: A formal קנין makes the full amount binding
steps.stepSummary: No contradiction: מרימר's case is where the husband made a קנין with the bride's father for the full amount. The ברייתא's case is where no קנין was made.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This is where they made a קנין with him, and that is where they did not make a קנין with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves רבינא's challenge by saying the two rulings speak about different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the extra amount is just for show, so the ברייתא limits the wife to the real portion. But if the groom's side made a קנין with the bride's father, the father is bound to give the full written sum. Then it is no longer for show but a real obligation, so מרימר lets her collect all of it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (the two sources do not truly conflict)
This case... that case (splitting the sources into different situations)
They made a formal act of acquisition (קנין) with him

steps.whatToRemember: A written amount that custom treats as just for honor is collected only at its real value, unless a formal קנין made the full amount binding.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where they performed an act of acquisition with him,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the round-bracket word and some have the square-bracket one. Either way, a קנין was made with the bride's father.

phrases.english: that is where they did not perform an act of acquisition with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the two rulings apply to different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מרימר seemed to contradict the ברייתא by giving the wife the inflated honor amount.
steps.terutzMaskana: מרימר speaks where a קנין made the full amount binding. The ברייתא speaks where no קנין was made, so only the real amount is owed.

steps.title: רבינא refuses to make a קנין on a doubled dowry
steps.stepSummary: רבינא wrote a doubled dowry for his daughter. When the groom's side asked for a קנין, he said it is either a קנין or a doubled number, never both.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא wrote an enhanced, doubled dowry amount for his daughter. They said to him: let us make a קנין with you for it. He said to them: if there is a קנין, I will not double the number. If I double the number, there will be no קנין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about רבינא that shows the rule from Step 5 in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 taught that a קנין makes the father owe the full written amount, even the extra added for honor. רבינא knew this, so he refused to make a קנין on a doubled number. A father may write the real amount and back it with a קנין, or write the doubled amount for honor without a קנין, but not both.

keyTerms.meaning: Enhancing: writing a bigger amount than what is really being given, for honor
Let us make a קנין, an act that makes the promise legally binding

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the difference between 'with a קנין' and 'without a קנין' from Step 5 is real and practical. A careful father guarded against owing the doubled amount.

phrases.english: Ravina enhanced and wrote for his daughter.
phrases.notes: He wrote a bigger dowry number than he was really giving, as the local custom did for honor.

phrases.english: They said to him: Let us make an act of acquisition with the Master.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אִי מִקְנֵא – לָא מִיכְפַּל,
phrases.english: He said to them: If there is an acquisition, it is not doubled;
if it is doubled, there is no acquisition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the קנין distinction from Step 5 being used in practice
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A קנין and a doubled dowry number do not go together. With a קנין, the written amount is fully owed.

steps.title: Does 400 in her כתובה mean real 400 or written 400?
steps.stepSummary: A man said to give his daughter 400 זוז in her כתובה. רב אחא בריה דרב אויא asks רב אשי whether that means a real 400 (written as 800) or a written 400 (really 200).
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain man who said to them: give my daughter four hundred זוז in her כתובה. רב אחא בריה דרב אויא sent a question to רב אשי: does he mean four hundred that are written as eight hundred, or four hundred written that are really two hundred?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a new case and asks how to understand the man's words. This sets up רב אשי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since custom doubles the dowry in the כתובה, the number 400 could mean two things. It could be the real amount, which would then be written as 800. Or it could be the written amount, which is really worth only 200. The question is which one the man meant.

keyTerms.meaning: The marriage document that records what the wife is owed

steps.confusionAlert: 'Four hundred that are eight hundred' does not mean she gets 800. It means she really gets 400, which the כתובה writes as 800 because of the doubling custom.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to them:
Give her four hundred zuz,
to my daughter, in her marriage contract.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַח רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rav Avya, sent
before Rav Ashi:
Four hundred that are eight hundred,
phrases.notes: He means a real 400, which would be written in the כתובה as 800.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אַרְבַּע מְאָה זוּזֵי דְּאִינּוּן מָאתַן?
phrases.english: or four hundred zuz that are two hundred?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the קנין question to a new case about how to read a man's instructions
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether '400 in her כתובה' means a real 400 or a written 400 that is really 200

steps.title: רב אשי: give her versus write for her
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that it depends on the wording. 'Give her' means a real 400. 'Write for her' means a written 400, which is really 200.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: we look at what he said. If he said 'give her,' it means four hundred real זוז, written as eight hundred. If he said 'write for her,' it means four hundred written זוז, which are really two hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question by looking at the man's exact verb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Give' is about real money handed over, so 400 is the true amount. 'Write' is about the number in the document, so 400 is the doubled number and the real value is half. This follows רבי יוסי's idea from Step 2: read words the way people normally use them.

keyTerms.meaning: We look and examine the wording

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: We look:
If he said "give her,"

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע מְאָה זוּזֵי דְּאִינּוּן תַּמְנֵי מְאָה,
phrases.english: it is four hundred zuz that are eight hundred;
if he said "write for her,"
it is four hundred zuz that are two hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 7
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Give her' means a real 400. 'Write for her' means a written 400 worth 200.

steps.title: Another version: for her כתובה versus in her כתובה
steps.stepSummary: A second version of רב אשי's answer makes the difference depend on 'לכתובתה' (for her כתובה) versus 'בכתובתה' (in her כתובה).
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב אשי said: we look. If he said 'for her כתובה,' it means a real four hundred, written as eight hundred. If he said 'in her כתובה,' it means four hundred written, which are really two hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different report of what רב אשי said. In this version, the key is a tiny word change, not 'give' versus 'write.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'For her כתובה' sounds like money given toward her dowry, so it is the real amount. 'In her כתובה' sounds like the number written inside the document, so it is the doubled number, worth half. The difference is only one letter: ל or ב.

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: חָזֵינַן
phrases.english: Some say: Rav Ashi said: We look:
If he said "for her marriage contract,"

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע מְאָה זוּזֵי דְּאִינּוּן תַּמְנֵי מְאָה,
phrases.english: it is four hundred zuz that are eight hundred;
and if he said "in her marriage contract,"
it is four hundred zuz that are two hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of רב אשי's answer to the same question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'For her כתובה' means a real 400. 'In her כתובה' means a written 400 worth 200.

steps.title: Rejecting the second version: only a plain give her means real money
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the second version. Whether he said 'for' or 'in' her כתובה, it means a written 400 worth 200. Only a plain 'give her,' with no mention of the כתובה, means a real 400.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is not so. It makes no difference whether he said 'for her כתובה' or 'in her כתובה.' Either way it is four hundred written, which are really two hundred, unless he said simply 'give her.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the ל-versus-ב difference from Step 9 and gives the final rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the man mentions the כתובה at all, his number is read as a כתובה number, so it is doubled and worth half. Only a plain 'give her' (הבו לה סתמא) with no mention of the כתובה means real money. This is stricter than the first version in Step 8, which counted 'give her' as real money even though this man also said 'in her כתובה.'

keyTerms.meaning: And that is not so: rejects the view just stated

steps.whatToRemember: Any mention of the כתובה makes the number a written, doubled amount worth half. Only a plain 'give her' means the full real amount.

phrases.english: And that is not so;
there is no difference whether he said "for her marriage contract"
or whether he said "in her marriage contract":
it is four hundred zuz that are two hundred,
unless he said "give her" plainly.
phrases.notes: Plainly means he did not mention the כתובה at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overrules the second version in Step 9 and sets the final rule
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the ל-versus-ב distinction in the second version of רב אשי
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Any mention of the כתובה, whether 'for' or 'in,' points to the written doubled number
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Only a plain 'give her' means a real 400. Any mention of the כתובה means 400 written, worth 200.

steps.title: The sharecropper who promised 1,000 זוז
steps.stepSummary: A sharecropper promised to pay 1,000 זוז if he left the field unworked, and then he left one third of it unworked.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man took a field to work from another man. He said: 'If I leave it unworked, I will give you 1,000 זוז.' He then left one third of the field unworked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about a sharecropper's penalty promise. This sets up the question of how much, if anything, he has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The promise was for leaving the field unworked, but he only neglected a third of it. Two questions come up: is the promise binding at all, and if it is, how much does he owe for a partial failure?

keyTerms.meaning: Took a field to work for the owner as a sharecropper
I leave it unworked (let it lie fallow)

phrases.english: There was a certain man who took land from his fellow,
phrases.notes: He took it as a sharecropper, meaning he works the field and splits the crop with the owner.

phrases.english: he said: If I leave it unworked,
I will give you a thousand זוז.
He left a third unworked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about a sharecropper's promise, moving away from the כתובה wording discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup: a 1,000 זוז penalty promise, with only a third of the field neglected.

steps.title: The נהרדעי: he pays one third
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים of נהרדעא rule that he pays 333⅓ זוז, a third of the promised amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים of נהרדעא said: The law is that he gives him 333⅓ זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: The נהרדעי give the first ruling on the case: the promise counts, and he pays in proportion to what he neglected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They treat the promise as a real, binding obligation. Since he neglected a third of the field, he pays a third of 1,000 זוז.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים of the city נהרדעא

phrases.english: The Sages of Neharde'a said:
The law is that he gives him
three hundred and thirty-three and a third.
phrases.notes: That is a third of 1,000, matching the third of the field he left unworked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first ruling on the case from step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The promise is binding. He pays in proportion: 333⅓ זוז for neglecting a third.

steps.title: רבא: the promise is not binding
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees and says the promise is an אסמכתא, and an אסמכתא does not create an obligation, so he pays nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is an אסמכתא, and an אסמכתא does not make a binding commitment.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second, opposite ruling: the promise is not binding at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אסמכתא is a promise a person makes because he is sure he will never have to pay it. He never really meant to commit, so the promise does not obligate him. This argues with the נהרדעי, who treated the promise as real.

keyTerms.meaning: A promise made only because the person is sure it will never come due, so it is not a real commitment
Does not acquire, meaning it does not create a binding obligation

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the sharecropper did nothing wrong. He is saying this specific penalty promise is not legally binding.

phrases.english: Rava said: It is an asmachta,
and an asmachta does not acquire.
phrases.notes: He means the promise does not obligate him, so he does not have to pay the 1,000 זוז or any part of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues with the נהרדעי's ruling in step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The promise is an אסמכתא and is not binding.

steps.title: Challenge to רבא from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבא's case differs from the משנה, where a sharecropper's promise to 'pay with the best' if he leaves the field unworked is binding.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבא, how is this different from what we learned in the משנה: 'If I leave it unworked and do not work it, I will pay with the best'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא. The משנה seems to treat a similar promise as binding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a sharecropper's promise to pay if he neglects the field is enforced. If that promise counts, why isn't the promise of 1,000 זוז just as binding?

phrases.english: And according to Rava, what is different
from that which we learned in the Mishnah:
"If I leave it unworked and do not work it,
phrases.notes: This is the wording from the משנה earlier on this daf, which a sharecropper writes into his contract.

phrases.english: I will pay with the best"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's ruling from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that a sharecropper's penalty promise is an אסמכתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה enforces a sharecropper's promise to pay if he neglects the field. That looks like the same kind of conditional promise, so it should also count as an אסמכתא, yet it is binding.

steps.title: Exaggerated versus normal promise
steps.stepSummary: In the משנה he did not exaggerate. Here he promised far more than the real loss, so it is just exaggeration and not binding.
steps.simpleTranslation: There he did not exaggerate. Here, since he said something extra, he is just exaggerating.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא by pointing out a difference between the two promises.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה he only promised to cover the owner's actual loss, using the best produce, which is a fair and real commitment. Promising 1,000 זוז goes far beyond the loss. That shows he was just talking big, which makes it an אסמכתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Exaggerates or makes an empty threat
Something extra, more than the real loss

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, a promise to cover the real loss is binding. A promise of an inflated amount is an אסמכתא and is not binding.

phrases.english: There he is not exaggerating;
here, since he said something extra,
phrases.notes: The 'extra' is the 1,000 זוז, which is far more than the owner would really lose.

phrases.english: it is mere exaggeration that he is saying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 14 and protects רבא's view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any sharecropper's conditional promise to pay should be treated the same, either all binding or all אסמכתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: A promise to pay the real loss is binding. An inflated promise is mere exaggeration and an אסמכתא.

steps.title: Wheat planted instead of sesame
steps.stepSummary: A sharecropper took land to plant sesame but planted wheat, and the wheat earned as much as sesame would have.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man took land to plant sesame, but he planted wheat. The wheat came out worth the same as sesame.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new sharecropper story. This sets up the question of whether the sharecropper gets anything extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sesame weakens the soil more than wheat. Here the owner got the same profit, and his land was spared damage. The question is whether the sharecropper deserves credit for that.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who took land to plant sesame,
he planted it with wheat.
The wheat produced like sesame.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, separate case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup: wheat planted instead of sesame, with the same profit.

steps.title: רב כהנא: credit for sparing the land
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא thought the sharecropper should be credited for the damage the sesame would have done to the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא thought to say that they reduce the owner's share by the amount the land would have been weakened.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives a first idea for this case. The words 'סבר... למימר' tell us this is only what he first thought, and it will be rejected next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His logic is that the owner got the same profit and also kept his soil stronger. So the sharecropper should get the value of that saved damage taken from the owner's share.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought to say (a first idea that is later rejected)

phrases.english: Rav Kahana thought to say
they deduct for him the weakening of the land.
phrases.notes: The owner's share is reduced, and the sharecropper is credited for the soil damage he saved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first ruling on the case from step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First thought: the sharecropper gets credit for the land damage he spared the owner.

steps.title: רב אשי: owners prefer money over land
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rejects רב כהנא using a popular saying: people would rather have the land weakened than have the owner lose money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to רב כהנא: People say, 'Let the land be weakened, but let its owner not be weakened.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back on רב כהנא's idea with a well-known saying about what owners really care about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Owners care more about income than about protecting their soil. So sparing the land is not a benefit the owner values, and the sharecropper gets no extra credit.
steps.whatToRemember: The sharecropper gets no credit for sparing the land, because owners value profit more than the strength of their soil.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Rav Kahana,
people say:
Let the land be weakened,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, meaning 'let it be weakened.'

phrases.english: and let its owner not be weakened.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא, אָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב כהנא's idea from step 17.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects giving the sharecropper credit for sparing the land.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב כהנא assumed the owner values protecting his soil. In reality owners care about profit, so the sharecropper gave him no benefit he values.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a benefit counts based on what owners actually care about, not just on what looks good on paper.

steps.title: A sharecropper plants wheat instead of sesame and earns more
steps.stepSummary: A sharecropper agreed to grow sesame, planted wheat instead, and the wheat earned more than sesame would have.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who took a field to plant sesame. He planted wheat, and the wheat earned more than sesame would have.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new real-life case that is close to the one in step 16. This step only sets out the facts, and the ruling comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 16 the wheat earned the same as sesame. Here the wheat earned more, so the new question is who gets the extra profit.

phrases.english: A certain man who received land to plant sesame,
planted it with wheat,
and it produced wheat worth more than sesame.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up to the case in step 16, but this time the wheat earned more than sesame instead of the same.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: the switched crop earned more than the agreed crop.

steps.title: רבינא thinks the sharecropper gets the extra profit
steps.stepSummary: רבינא thought the owner must give the sharecropper the difference between the wheat's value and the sesame's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא wanted to say that the owner gives the sharecropper the extra amount in between.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא suggests a ruling: the sharecropper keeps all the extra profit that came from switching crops.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא's reasoning is that the sharecropper's switch to wheat caused the gain, so the gain should be his. The word סבר ('he thought') hints that this view is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: he thought, he was inclined to say (often a view that gets rejected)

phrases.english: Ravina thought to say
that he gives him the added value that is in between.
phrases.notes: 'In between' means the gap between what the wheat earned and what sesame would have earned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first ruling on the case just described.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sharecropper receives the full difference between the wheat's value and the sesame's value.

steps.title: רב אחא מדפתי says the land helped too
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי rejects רבינא: the land also produced the extra gain, so the sharecropper cannot claim all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדפתי said to רבינא: Did only he make it better? Didn't the land make it better too?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא מדפתי pushes back on רבינא with a sharp question. The extra profit did not come from the sharecropper alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא gave all the gain to the sharecropper's choice. רב אחא points out that the owner's land also produced that gain, so the extra should not go to the sharecropper alone and the owner deserves a share.

keyTerms.meaning: is that to say? (a question that rejects an idea)
he improved, he made it worth more

steps.whatToRemember: In the sharecropper cases, the land counts as a real partner in any gain, so extra profit from a switched crop is not the sharecropper's alone.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa of Difti said to Ravina:
Is that to say that he alone improved it,
and the land did not improve it?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ הוּא אַשְׁבַּח, אַרְעָא לָא אַשְׁבַּחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבינא's ruling from step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבינא's view that the sharecropper takes all of the extra value.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It ignores the land's part in producing the gain.

steps.title: נהרדעי: an עיסקא is half loan and half deposit
steps.stepSummary: נהרדעי rule that an עיסקא business arrangement counts as half a loan and half a deposit, a fair middle ground for both sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים of נהרדעא said: This business deal is half a loan and half a deposit. The רבנן made a rule that works well for the borrower and works well for the lender.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic, the עיסקא, where one person gives money and another does business with it. נהרדעי define its legal status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan belongs fully to the borrower, and he carries all the risk. A deposit stays the owner's, and the keeper does not carry the risk of an accident. Making it half and half splits the risk and the rights, so both sides are treated fairly.

keyTerms.meaning: a business deal where one gives money and the other does business with it
a deposit kept for the owner
the Sages of the city נהרדעא
it is good for him, it suits him

steps.confusionAlert: The 'borrower' (לוה) here is the manager who does the business. The 'lender' (מלוה) is the investor who gave the money.
steps.whyThisMatters: This half loan, half deposit definition is the base for every question that follows about what the manager may do with the money.

phrases.english: The Sages of Neharde'a say:
This business venture
is half a loan and half a deposit,
the Rabbis made an arrangement
that is good for the borrower
and good for the lender.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי נְהַרְדָּעֵי: הַאי עִיסְקָא פַּלְגָא מִלְוָה וּפַלְגָא פִּקָּדוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, moving from sharecropping to business partnerships.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עיסקא is treated as half loan and half deposit, balancing the interests of both sides.

steps.title: Since half is a loan, the manager may spend it on drink
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reasons that because half is a loan, the manager may spend that half however he likes, even on beer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that we said half is a loan, if he wants to drink beer with it, that is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a practical result from the 'half loan' idea: a loan belongs to the borrower, so he can use that half as he wishes. This sets up רבא's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower owns loaned money and may spend it on anything as long as he pays it back later. If half the עיסקא is a real loan, the manager should have that same freedom over that half.

keyTerms.meaning: now that we have said (introduces a result of an earlier rule)
it is fine, it is allowed

phrases.english: Now that we have said that half is a loan,
if he wants to drink beer with it,
it is fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical result from נהרדעי's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The manager may use the loan half for anything, even drink.

steps.title: רבא: the name עיסקא means it is for business only
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects this. The money is called עיסקא ('business') because the investor can say it was given only for doing business, not for drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: That is why it is called עיסקא, since the investor can say to him: I gave it to you to do business with, not to drink beer with.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on the idea that the manager may spend the loan half freely. He proves his point from the name of the deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though half is called a loan, the whole deal was made for business. The name עיסקא shows the money has a set purpose, so the manager is limited to using it for trade.

phrases.english: Rava said:
For this reason they call it a 'business venture,'
because he can say to him:
When I gave it to you, it was to do business with it,
and not to drink beer with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: לְהָכִי קָרוּ לֵיהּ עִיסְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the result drawn in step 23.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the manager may spend the loan half freely.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It treats the loan half like an ordinary loan and ignores that the whole deal exists for business.

steps.title: רב אידי בר אבין: if the manager dies, the money becomes his children's movables
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין says that if the manager dies, the loan half becomes movable property in his children's hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said: And if he dies, it becomes movable property with his children.
steps.whatsHappening: A second result of the 'half loan' idea is offered, this time about what happens after the manager dies. This sets up רבא's second reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If half is a real loan, then after the manager dies that money is simply his heirs' מטלטלין. A lender normally cannot collect a debt from movables that יתומים inherited, so the investor would lose that half.

keyTerms.meaning: in the hands of his children

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said:
And if he died,
it becomes movable property with his children.
phrases.notes: The point is that a lender can't collect from movables that the children inherited, so the investor would lose the loan half.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין: וְאִם מֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second practical result drawn from נהרדעי's 'half loan' ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the manager's death, the loan half becomes his heirs' movable property, which the investor cannot collect.

steps.title: רבא: the name עיסקא keeps it from becoming the children's movables
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects this too. The deal is called עיסקא exactly so that if the manager dies, the money does not become his children's movables.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: That is why it is called עיסקא, so that if he dies it does not become movable property with his children.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא again uses the name עיסקא to block a result of the 'half loan' idea. This time it protects the investor after the manager dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because it is a business arrangement and not a plain loan, the money keeps its identity as the investment. It does not become the heirs' ordinary movables, so the investor can still claim it.
steps.whatToRemember: An עיסקא is half loan and half deposit, but רבא twice shows from its name that it is a business arrangement. The manager may not spend it on personal things, and it does not become his children's movables when he dies.

phrases.english: Rava said:
For this reason they call it a business venture,
so that if he dies
it does not become movable property with his children.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: לְהָכִי קָרוּ לֵיהּ עִיסְקָא, דְּאִם מֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב אידי בר אבין's result from step 25, using the same reasoning as step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the loan half becomes the heirs' uncollectable movables.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It treats the עיסקא as an ordinary loan, when the name shows it is a business arrangement that keeps its identity.

steps.title: One business deal written in two documents is the lender's loss
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that when one עיסקא is written up as two separate שטרות, each is judged on its own, and this works against the מלוה (the investor).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says: If there is one business deal but two documents, the loss falls on the lender.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new rule. When an investor and a manager write one business deal into two separate documents, the investor (the מלוה) ends up losing out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because there are two documents, each one counts as its own separate deal. A loss in one deal is not balanced against a gain in the other. Under the usual עיסקא terms, the investor takes his share of the gain from one deal and also carries the heavy loss of the other, which is bad for him.

keyTerms.meaning: The lender, meaning here the investor who gave the money

steps.confusionAlert: Here מלוה means the investor who supplied the money, not a regular lender in a simple loan. He is called that because half of the עיסקא counts as a loan.
steps.whatToRemember: Two documents make two separate deals. Their gains and losses are not added together, and that hurts the investor (the מלוה).
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the way a deal is written down can change how profit and loss are divided, even when the business itself is really a single venture.

phrases.english: Rava says:
One business deal and two documents:
phrases.notes: He means one venture that was written up as two separate deals of equal value. One of them lost a lot and the other gained a little.

phrases.english: It is the lender's loss.
phrases.notes: Each document is settled on its own, so the losses of one aren't balanced against the gains of the other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: חֲדָא עִיסְקָא וּתְרֵי שְׁטָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting two conclusions drawn from the 'half loan, half deposit' rule (steps 24 and 26), רבא adds a new practical rule about how עיסקא documents are treated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One עיסקא written in two separate documents is treated as two separate deals. Profits and losses are not combined, which works out to the loss of the investor (the מלוה).
